extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political philosophy, social science, and methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and principles for forming a deductive science of character (Ethology) and for methodological conduct in the social sciences, emphasizing when deduction vs. induction is appropriate and limits of experimental methods. Advises on how to derive middle principles from general laws and how to verify theoretical deductions against experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethology as a deductive science (Science of Character)
rubrics_metrics.description: A science is thus formed, to which I would propose to give the name of Ethology, or the Science of Character ... Ethology, as I have conceived it, is, as I have already remarked, altogether deductive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethology should deduce the laws of formation of character from the general laws of mind (Psychology). It corresponds to the art of education and treats complex social effects as corollaries of simpler psychological laws; theoretical deductions should be worked out and then compared with empirical generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific propositions should assert tendencies, not certainties
rubrics_metrics.description: They must not assert that something will always, or certainly, happen; but only that such and such will be the effect of a given cause, so far as it operates uncounteracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame propositions as tendencies (e.g., 'bodily strength tends to make men courageous') rather than universal laws. Recognize that tendencies may be frustrated by other causes; this preserves scientific generality while acknowledging contingency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate simple cases (analysis of component causes) before complex phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: that which tries its experiments not on the complex facts, but on the simple ones of which they are compounded; and after ascertaining the laws of the causes, the composition of which gives rise to the complex phenomena, then considers whether these will not explain ... the sequences of those complex phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design inquiries to isolate and understand simple component causes; deduce how their composition produces complex social outcomes. Use analysis of simple cases as the basis for explaining empirically observed complex regularities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethology as middle principles (axiomata media) derived from Psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: The principles of Ethology are properly the middle principles, the axiomata media (as Bacon would have said) of the science of mind: as distinguished ... from the empirical laws ... and ... from the highest generalizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on deriving and organizing middle-level principles that connect general psychological laws to observable social effects. These middle principles are of principal practical value for explanation and application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification a posteriori must proceed pari passu with deduction a priori
rubrics_metrics.description: It is hardly necessary again to repeat, that, as in every other deductive science, verification à posteriori must proceed pari passu with deduction à priori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always test theoretical deductions against specific experience; do not accept deductions without empirical verification, nor observations without theoretical affiliation. The 'consilience' of a priori reasoning and a posteriori evidence is the sufficient ground for principles in complex sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain truths most amenable to real induction first; no rigid order
rubrics_metrics.description: The order in which truths of the various degrees of generality should be ascertained, cannot, I apprehend, be prescribed by any unbending rule. I know of no maxim ... but to obtain those first, in respect to which the conditions of a real induction can be first and most completely realized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the sequence of inquiry pragmatically: pursue those generalizations for which reliable inductive conditions exist. Where causes are accessible, start with simplest cases which yield broad laws; sometimes highest generalizations emerge earliest and can be used deductively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science may yield laws without universal practical precepts; adapt art to circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary even to the perfection of a science, that the corresponding art should possess universal, or even general, rules. ... the art might not have a single general precept to give, except that of watching the circumstances of the particular case, and adapting our measures to the effects ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that applied practice (politics, education) often requires case-by-case adaptation. Use scientific laws to inform judgment about tendencies and suitable interventions, then translate principles into context-sensitive precepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of Causes: social phenomena reduce to individual human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: In social phenomena the Composition of Causes is the universal law. Human beings in society have no properties but those which are derived from, and may be resolved into, the laws of the nature of individual man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze social phenomena by decomposing them into the actions and passions of individuals governed by psychological laws. Do not treat society as a fundamentally different substance with independent properties; look for constituent human causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental/Chemical method is inappropriate for social science
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of philosophizing which may be termed chemical overlooks this fact, and proceeds as if the nature of man as an individual were not concerned at all ... they profess to demand, in all cases without exception, specific experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of treating political facts as if they were chemical experiments; you cannot perform controlled artificial experiments on societies, and unanalysed historical instances are inadequate for conclusive induction because of pervasive confounding causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference impracticable for national-level social inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to apply to the case the most perfect of the methods of experimental inquiry, the Method of Difference, we require to find two instances, which tally in every particular except the one which is the subject of inquiry. ... The supposition that two such instances can be met with is manifestly absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on finding two nations/societies identical except for one institutional difference; differences in legislation are themselves effects of prior causes, so the strict Method of Difference cannot be applied to most social questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect Method of Difference is inconclusive in plural-cause settings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Indirect Method of Difference ... compares two classes of instances respectively agreeing in nothing but the presence of a circumstance on the one side and its absence on the other. Yet, that it is inconclusive, scarcely requires to be pointed out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparing one restrictive country with several free-trade countries cannot reliably isolate causal effect because prosperity may be due to the aggregation of many favourable circumstances. Indirect comparisons can suggest but not prove causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement and Concomitant Variations unreliable with plurality of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: But we are already aware of how little value this method is, in cases admitting Plurality of Causes ... Similar objections will be found to apply to the Method of Concomitant Variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminating some antecedents does not show that a remaining antecedent is non-instrumental; concurrent multiple causes mean agreement and concomitant variation methods have very limited inferential power in social phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Residues has limited, cautious applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: There remains the Method of Residues; which appears, on the first view, less foreign to this kind of inquiry ... Making allowance, thereupon, for the effect of all causes whose tendencies are known, the residue which those causes are inadequate to explain may plausibly be imputed to the remainder ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method of Residues can be used when one can reasonably account for known causes and attribute unexplained effects to remaining factors, but its conclusions are tentative. Accurate noting and accounting of circumstances is required; use with caution and seek corroboration.
